metas.name: Assam  - Assamese
metas.note: Assamese, mainly found in Assam, also uses the Bengali script, with the addition of some characters, most notably ৰ and ৱ.
metas.footer: Check out https://www.plonkit.net/ for more clues.

metas.name: Gujarat  - Gujarati
metas.note: Gujarati, found in Gujarat, has a script with several similarities to the Hindi script, however it notably lacks the horizontal line at the top of every word.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Karnataka  - Kannada
metas.note: Kannada is found in Karnataka and has a script with a lot of smooth curves and small circles. It is very similar to the Telugu script, with Telugu having one additional feature described in the next tip. Many characters also feature a distinct squiggly tail in the top right corner, which is less common in Telugu.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Kerala  - Malayalam
metas.note: The Malayalam script can be found in Kerala and mostly consists of somewhat simple-looking curvy letters, often containing upside-down U-shapes.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Maharashtra  - Marathi
metas.note: Marathi, found in Maharashtra, also uses the Devanagari script, however it sometimes uses the letter ळ which is not found in Hindi.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Manipur  - Manipuri
metas.note: Manipuri, also called Meitei, is the official language of Manipur. It is written using the Meitei script, which can be recognised by its many vertical lines and right angles.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Mizoram  - Mizo
metas.note: Mizo, found in Mizoram, is the language most commonly found on the Indian coverage other than English, which uses the Latin script
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: North & Central India  - Hindi
metas.note: Hindi is the most common language in India and can be found in many central and northern regions. It uses the Devanagari script, which can be recognised by the line going through the top of each word and the straight vertical lines found in the majority of all letters.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Odisha  - Oriya
metas.note: The Oriya script is found in Odisha and has a curvy look, with many letters having wide semi-circles covering the top. Many letters have a distinct diacritic in the shape of a wide curve above the top of the letter. A useful mnemonic is that the shape of the characters resembles a skull emoji
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Punjab  - Punjabi
metas.note: Punjabi can be found in Punjab in northwestern India. While the script looks somewhat similar to Hindi, it can generally be differentiated by the softer shape of the letters and the horizontal bar being broken over certain letters. It also has some distinctly different features, such as the letters ਨ, ਲ and ਅ as well as a diacritic in the shape of a soft curve beneath a letter.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Tamil Nadu  - Tamil
metas.note:
The Tamil script is found in Tamil Nadu and has a distinct combination of curves, straight lines and 90° angles. Some letters also have diacritics shaped like dots.

NOTE: Tamil is also commonly found in Sri Lanka.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: Telangana & Andhra Pradesh  - Telugu
metas.note: Telugu, found in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, has a script very similar to Kannada, but you’ll often see diacritics resembling checkmarks at the top of letters.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.

metas.name: West Bengal & Tripura  - Bengali
metas.note:
Bengali is found in northeastern India and has a similar look to Devanagari (Hindi), however it can usually be recognised by the many letters featuring left-facing triangular shapes.

NOTE: This is also the language found in Bangladesh.
metas.footer: Description and images taken from: https://www.plonkit.net/.
